div.head: PRIZE FISH SIOUX.
div.p: THE PRIZE FISH SIOUX.

The "New York Evening World" recently offered a I prize for the best fish story, and Mr. J. L. 6 untikel, of Toledo, Ohio,Wo,ll the wire with this yarn was inn boat off Edgewater, on 'remade Creek, a tributary to Lake Eris, fishing for perch. Near the will rice on the opposite side of the stream I noticed every now and then the splash of a large fish ; and thinking there might be a hungry pike feeding, I changed Inv tackle, hooked a Sin. perch securely bohinil the aorsal fin, and made a east. A heavy strike, the reel spun, and a second strike folldwed. The movement of : ' the fish ceased, and a trembling sensation in the line and rod Woo experienced, which mired to the este.: tie of the stream, and a regular shakingensued, resembli ing a terrier worrying a rat. I gave a jerk—no effect ; the sensation continued the more savagely ; it felt very heavy. Gradually I hauled Mond when within a few feet of my boat loan the trouble. A 911,. pike had a wtvage holirof the head of the perch, a 71b. dogfish a hold if the tail, and the hook remained in its original position between the heads of the two fish who Were struggling for the perch, and IMO continued after I landed them, and neither would let go the hilt. The two large fish were caught without the hook touching either.

div.head: BRIDGEWATER NAVIGATION
div.p: THE BRIDGEWATER NAVIGATION
COMPANY. A PLETHORA OF FUNDS.

..... _ _ In the llou.e of Lords, on Tuesday, the appeal was argued which raised an important question as to the distribution of the money paid to the bridge- water Navigal ion Company, now being voluntarily wound up. The company was bought by the Man- chester Ship Canal Company, and the sum paid was sullicient to enable the Bridgewater Company to return the whole of the paid-up capital, both ordinary and preference, leaving a large surplus. The question was how that surplus was to be divided. The shares were £lO, lint they were divided in this way. The ordinary allures were of LIP, with 10s. pail while in the ease of the ! preference shares, the whole of the £lO had been paid, and the question was how, as between those two, was the surplus to be divided. Mr. Justice North decided that it was to be divided between the preference and the ordinary share- holders in accordance with the sums which they had paid up, and the Court of Appeal upheld that decision. The present appeal was taken by Mr. Thomas Henry Birch, of Manchester, as representing the ordinary shareholders. The whole of the undertakings of the company having been taken away, nothing remained Inn to wind up and divide the surplus. The contending parties were the holders of 30,000 preference shares, and the ordinary shareholders, the latter contending that the utmost the preference shareholders were entitled to was the capital they advanced, with 5 per cent. The ordinary shareholdersrested their claims on two propositions—that the preference shareholders were not really shareholders at all, as the issue of the shares to them was ultra rite's, and when they got back the money with interest that was all they were entitled to ; and secondly, that if they were shareholders, their share of the profit was limited by contract in the article to 5 per cent.. and that by ' Ike contract theordinary shareholders were entitled to all the other protits, including all profile arising from the increase in the value of its property. Sir ' Horace Davey argued the Circe for the appellants, and Mr. Rigby for the revoratents, but the case had not concluded when their lordships adjourned.

div.head: COST OF ROYALTY.
div.p: THE COST OF ROYALTY.

It is a vers. Alitlicoit thing to ascertain the annual cost of the Royal Family. And n real account is ever given Ito the nation of thin most important matter. The pay.- , Inents made are not inclusive, Tht, Civil List, which
suppesed to to a lu.n:p sum including everything, dces n.d really cover half the total cost. Thousands of pounds are scattered tip and down the Estimates which

really ought to go lODIeI the Civil List. Even if we put the Civil List of £385,000 and the annuities to the Royal Family of £158,009 together, they do not represent the aggregate cost. And just as there is no method of measuring the amount, which is variously estimated Iron) £700,000 to £BOO,OOO or a million a year, there in no method of comparing the expenditure of this and of previous reigns. The Civil List of William IV. was fixed at £700,000 a year, but it included a vast number of payments for perpetual and other pensions, diplomatic and consular expenditur, salaries of Ministers of State, and a huge number of miscellaneous items, not one of which are included in the £385,000 a year tee give to the Queen. The Civil List does not include the cost of repairs to palaces. the of the Duchy of Lancaster (now treated as the private property of the Queen, but until the reign of William IV, always treated as national property), the co.st of reyalyachts, military aides-de-camp, Crown parks and gardens, and a number of RIDICULOUS AND thivolors ENTERNES, from that of her Majesty's ekickmaker to the tuthcock and rat-catcher at Buckingham Palace. It does not elude even the nominal £lOO,OOO a year we give the Prince of Wales, and a large number of other payments we Inake on his tehalf, 00 any of the other royal dowrim and allowances which, aceordino to the Fin,r,ial Ikt;wo Almarmek, hove loin made to 'the Prince Consort and the nine children of the Queen. MI,. according to the same authority, have cost us in all £1,981,083. The Royal Family is also a rent-free lumily; it has hail all its steam fares to the Continent paid for it. It contri- butes nothing to the local or imperial revenue in the shape of ratio and taxes, and it claims all sorts of mysterious exemptions. .Thd Civil List excludes front view the not sums of money which mombers of the almost endless Royal Family' who have died in the prisont reign have drawn from the Exchequer, SUCII as the Queen's uncle, the Duke of Mosses; lot 011. King of Hanover, who Med in 1851, and drew over is milli in; lIIT aunt Queen Adelaide, who died in 1849, and drew £1,200,000; and her aunt, the Ductless of Cambridge, who died the other month, and drew in all £222,000. . .

SAD !WAVE IN INDIA,

A short time ago we gave some particulars of the career of Mr. Croloy, Inspector ,if hods in India, who is a Warrington man. We have now to record , the sad death of his .111 Albert, who seas a promising young fellow of twenty years of age. We take the details from the "The Deccan Times of Thursday, I June 20th -- A COIIIII,6PONDENT FROM I.llrIODEItlillArT writes: - Quite a gloom lias been cast over the place by the announcement this morning, of the death of Albert Croley (Bertio the eldest sou of Mr. Crolev, Inspector of Schools. Some three weeks ago this dear lad with some ten or twelve others, mad.. up a swimming party and early in the morn- ing were seen at the Mahe Saib's Tank- better known as the African Cavalry Tank. While bath- ing Bertie Croley mails up his mind to swim across the tank and return. Ile started from the band side, and when on his return journey, he got entangled in the weeds in the centre of the tank. Ms cries of distress alarmed the other lads on the bundoome of whom ran away through fright. There was no one to go to his rescue when Trooper Malionied- bin-Oomer of A. C. Guards, who was on his way to the let Lancer lines on the other side of the tank, heanl the screams of the two younger Croleys. The man took in the position at once and rushed to the rescue. With great presence of mind, he took with him a log or catamaran used by the Trumpeters of the Regiment for duck shooting, and reached young Croley just in time to seize him as he was sinking for the last time. Placing the unconscious boy on the log, he pushed it along to the shore. By this time the Officers of the Regiment and a crowd had gathered, and the lad was taken to the Regimental Hospital, when,after being properly attended to, he was restored to conscimisness and after a while taken home. Now comes the sad portion of my story--af tee such a rewire by a brave siddee, poor Bertie Cmley took bad with fever, followed by inflammation of the lungs, and, although every effort was made by Drs. Lawrie. Greany, and liehir to save this young life—he was only twenty last birthday—he sank this morning. Bertie Croley was a very promising boy, and was liked by all for his pleasant manner. Ile was attending the Gar- rison Riding School, where he was making rapid progress. Tall of stature and well proportioned. the boy would have made a good soldier—but alas ! it was his lot to be called in the tlower of his youth. ;The sorrowing parents have the sympathy of the ; whole community at the and loss they have sus- tamed

div.head: ROYAL GRANTS COMMITTEE.
div.p: ROYAL GRANTS COMMITTEE.

The report of the Select Committee on Royal 11 Grants was presented to the house of Commons on Monday night. After setting forth the course which has been adopted since the secession of the House of Hanover, the Committee express the opinion that the Queen would have a claim on the liberality of Parliament :dinolit she think fit to apply for such grants as, in accordance with precedent, may be- COMP requisite for the support of the Royal Family. her Majesty, however, has intimated that she did I not intend to press this claim for the children of her daughters and younger eons, and with regard to future sovereigns the Committee suggest that at the proper time arrangements should Inc made minter which no future claim of a similar kind can arise.l The Committee recommend that during the present reign the allowance to the l'rince of Wales should be ineniased .rnil.ooo per annum, his Royal Dieh- -1 ness making such provision for his children as he I may think fit. It is stated by a news agency that the amount originally proposed to be added to the Heir Apparent's annual income was £40,000, and that it was reduced to £36,1100 online proposition of Sir, Gladstone. Some other counter proposals of Mr. Gladstone's were rejected, but the right hon. gentleman voted with the Government on the motion for the adoption of the report, whilst Mr. Morley voted with the minority. A Parliamentary paper issued on Tuesday night contains the report of the Royal Grants Committee, including the draft report presented by Mr. Labon- I chere. which was rejected by 10 to 2. This draft I report enumerated the grants made to members of the Royal Family during the Queen's reign, and pointed out how largely of late years the revenues! of the Duchy of Lancaster and the Duchy of Corn- , wall, received by the Queen and the Prince of Wales respectively, had increased. There were, it was con- tended, ample funds belonging to the Queen and the Prince of Wales from which provision could be made for the children of the latter during the Queen's lifetime. The emphatic opinion if, recorded that the cost of maintenance of the Royal Family is already so great that in no circumstances should it be increased.

SIR W. HARCOURT ON THE PROPOSED GRANTS. Sir W. Harcourt, speaking at Hereford, on Wednesday night, ridiculed Mr. Goscheresassertion that the Liberal party was downcast. Month after month they were repaving fresh assurances of the support of the country, fresh signs that the coercive policy of the Government was being condemned, and that the coastithencies were Irallying round the party in favour of conciliation and peace. After answering some of the popular objections to Hon, Role, and arguing in particular that the agrarian difficulty in Ireland was caushl by political ntisgoverno ()lent, Sir W. Harcourt denied that the grant of Home Rule would necessitate a recasting ..f the British consti- tution. The present Parliament would remain just what ' it was. Speaking on Royal grants, Sir William Harcourt complained of the conduct of her Majesty's Government in that they had placed in a very false peation both the Crown anti the House of Comnonons. (('heers.) They , originally propovd a set of nvolutions which, to put it shortly, proposed to give £50,000 a year in various sums to the children of the Prince of Wales. Well, that was a larger sum than was given out of the Consolidated ; Fund to the Prince and Princess of Wales them,tlves and I their original proposal involved this alas, that there I should be grants made fotthe children of other sons of the Queen, excepting those whn succeeded to foreign princes, In fact, it was an Assertion of the duty of the country to provide for all the grandeloiltintn of the Sovereign. These propo..ls, brought forward by the responsible Ministers of the Crown, awl which would be found in the report of the committee, were, when they came to be examined, so monstrous that they were withdrawn almost as soon as they were proposed. Tlut was a very false step. A responsible Government had no right to make, in the name of the Sovereign, claims; which they were not prepAred in every word to defend (hear, hear). That was, inderil, placing both the Crown I and the House of Commons in a totally false position. I They withdrew their proposals, and then thoy proposed I a Intim stun of £40,000 a year to be placed in trust of the Prince of Wales, to be distributed among the child- ren ; and having proposed £40,000 they agreed to aceer £36,000 a year, in lieu of £50,000 as original proposed. But they accompanied this with a declara- tion that the Sovereign hada claim on the liberality of the Government, should she think fit to apply for such, which in accordance with precedent, may become requisite for the support of the Royal family. he should like to ask, if it was a good claim, why was it waived? If it was not a good claim, why cast it ...Mal ? They were told that they need not mind the assertion of the claim, As for the moment it was waived; but the asser- tion might be made in the future, and this wen a point which would have to he detennined. It was clear, as the matter stood, that when another civil list came to be settled a claim may be net up in imitation of that which was HOW being waived. It was a complicated matter, but it WILS very important. What the Government should have done was To hare made a proposal to Parlia- ment, which should have been a complete and hnal settlement of this question. What they had done, how- ever, had Pon to make proposals whielt they could not defend ; and when Mr. Gladstone proposed amendments they aempted his proposal, but rejected his reason, while they ao the same time kept their town ntoxsom for their own proven]. which they abandoned. A more mutates- manlike muddle it was impossible to conceive. Mr. Gladstone's moderate statement was rejected ; that statement would have excluded all future claims. (Cheers.) The question now wa.s, what was to be in the matter ? He (Sir William) agreed very much with Mr. John Morley. The present proposal, coupled as it was with the reason)), which were given for it, and the claims attached to it, must be respected. If suclo a proposal were to in. carried, it must be accompanied by a declaration that thi”hould be the last grant in the present reign. (Cheers.) He did not see how it was possible for a photon.' %owl( as that put forward to be accepted on the part of the Government, and arm. hauled by a declaration which left everything unsettled and the future open to fresh demands. (Clestrs.) Sir ,million Harcourt's mewl) W. well received arld a resolotion denottincie,.. the Irish policy of the present 6.41'11111Pa Was passed unanimonsly.

div.head: MAYBRICK TRIAL.
div.p: THE MAYBRICK TRIAL.

A London correspondent telegriphed on Tuesday night: —Sir Charles Russell, who has accepted a special retainer to defend Mrs. Maybrick at the Liverpoill Assifss,had an interview this evening with Mr. Addison, who urosecutes for the Crown ; and it was decided that, subject to the approval of the judge, the trial shall be taken on the 31st inst. The learned counsel expect that the case will last • over three days. The principal witness for the defence will be the American gentleman. who, as I informed you some weeks ag., would testify that Mr.Marbrick, whilst !for a short tine, nsolent in the Unites! Si ides, was in ' the constant habit of taking arsenic. In support of this • testimony, there will be produced the original prescrip• Lion handed in by Mr. Mavbrick ton local chemist and dispensed by him ; and one of the witnesses will be Dr. Tidy, the celebrated chemist, wlm will he called to prove that the postonnebbs examination did not bear out the : allegations of the prosecutions.

WARRINGTON FIELD CUB. The following was the official programme of the ramble of the above-named club on Saturday:— Start from Museum at 3 p.m. footpath to Walton Arches. In pond in Bird Wood-lane, Water Soldier and Branched Bur-reed in Hower and probably Frog-bit. In field near do. Hemp-nettle (li. versi- color). Morley Common : Cranberry in fruit and Sundew (round leaved) in Hower. Cross Common to canal and forward to bower Walton. At Walton : Old Hall the chairman of the club (Mr. F. W. : Monks) will entertain the members to tea at five I o'clock.

In compliance with the above official no!ice and programme, the members of the Warrington Field Club met at the Moscow at 3 o'clock on Saturday afternoon. It was an extra or intercalary excursion not upon the summer programme. From Bold-st. the club wended its way across the tran.dlgured face of navvy-invaded .Arpley to Walton Bridges, where they were met by their chairman and enter- tainer of the evening. Thence along the Old Quay canal bank to a temporary wooden bridge across the canal leading to Bird Wood-lane. In two ponds on the right were found two out of the three British representatives of the natural order hydrocharidaos. Perhaps it would be nearer the truth to say that all the truly British species of the order are here repre- sented by the two very interesting plants the water soidier—rtratinter steed..., and the frog-bit -11ydrd- eharis morsus-rame. The other member of this interesting trio is an American plant, ansehares aldnastrust —the American water weed formerly so very abundant in the ponds in Arpley and , introduced into England no one seems to know bow, when, or why. All the three are floating: plants inhabiting ahallow pools and rending down radicles into the mud. The water-soldier, as its specific name implieB,very much resembles the aloes, a plant whose prodacts are not entirely unknown in St. Helens. The other "quite English" repre- sentative—the frog-hit--it a very intererting plant and well worth study by those whose minds have the botanic bent. It propagates its species not merely by seed, but by germination or budding. These buds sink to the bottom into the mud, where they lie daring the winter. In spring they rise to Ike surface, expand their leaves—flower and follow in the steps of their parents. (An interesting and instructive paper on this plant may be found in the 'Record" of the Warrington Field Naturalists' Society by Mr. James Cash, now in our library.) On Morley Cammon the scull cap, the cranberry in fruit, were duly noted and the party proceeded to the Ship Canal, where a fine section of descriptive upheaval was observed on the left bank of the canal. The crevices so formed had been subsequently filled by a lighter coloured material. From here the chair- man led the membms by deviolis and pleasant paths to the Old Hall of Walton, now renovated beyond recognition. The fifteen members of the club then attempted to do justice tothe excellent tea to which they were asked by Mr. and Mrs. F. W. Monks. Mr. Madeley, in a few appropriate words, proposed the heartiest thanks of the club to Mrs. NI onks for her hinds 'es, seconded by Mr. Peers,and carried by acclamation. Thus the club found " frcsli woods land past tires new."

On every side were signs of a terrific struggle having tales isla-ce. On the jury Morn- ing to the hotel, the Coroner said they were met to inquire into the death of Walter Davies, believed to be aged about 21 years, who was found stead in the cellar at 29, Market-nt., Atherton, at nine o'clock, or directly ' after, on Monday morning. It was palpablethat he had : died from violence either at his own hands or at the hands of someone else. Jaseph liavieo, the brother,,! the stemmed, has made the following stabanent in emnpany with nay mother, left Widnes by the 10.30 train, and arrived at Atherton about a quartersletst two. We then went to the house where Inv brother lodged with a Mrs. Hodgson. I VOldst I wasthere a sergeant gd police came in, and I then examined my brother, and found a terrible wound on the forehead about two Molest long, running down tothe right eyebrow. The wound would be fully half an inch deep. The pre]. try proceedings in connection with the trial of the Bishop of Lino du have advanced a stage this week. It has been ruled that a bishop in included in the words "all and singalar minis- tern" in the statutes of Elizabeth and Charles 11 ; so that a bishop cannot set himself almye the Act of Uniformity. The next step will, it is stated, In. taken inn october. Trying a bishop must be proceeded with slowly and solemnly; there must ho no inde,nt haste. The oriestion of cheap Sunday trains keeps cropping up—in the south as well as in the north. At the bah-yearly meeting of the London, Brigh- ton, and Smith Oast Railway Company a resolu- tion condemning Sunday excursions was brought forward, but it wan defeated by a large majority. Why should objection he taken to trains because they are cheap If it is a permissible thing to travel by rail on Sundap, it is equally permissible whether the rate be a halfpenny or a penny a toile.

ROMANTIC SUICIDE OF TWO LOVERS.

Joseph Harvey and Elizabeth Estes, aged twenty-one and twenty-two respectively, both residing at Langley- green, near Oldbury, were found drowned on Monday afternoon in the Canal Company S reservoir at Titford umler circumstances which show that they had together committml suicide. A note which they left stated that they had determined to die together in consequence of mutual love affairs and grievances as lovers.

div.head: SW EDIEF. HIGH LIFE TRACEDY.
div.p: SW EDIEF. HIGH LIFE TRACEDY.

BURNLEY GAZETTE, February 23rd. GilE lot of those who toil from day to day in the bowels of the earth is not a very agreeable one. Apart from the terrible risks of which we are so often reminded by a calamitous explosion,

with all its thrilling scenes, the collier has to pursue his 'work at times under circumstances of great hardship.. Mr. Moses Knowles, of 109, Oxford Road, Burnley, has had some experience of the trying conditions of labour in some of the deeper coal mines of this country. He relates how he has repeatedly had to work for hours crouched in ten or twelve inches of water and the cold liquid at the same time dropping all over his body from above. Happily such conditions of employment are almost unknown in the Burnley district, but Mr. Knowles has had to encounter them in other mining sufferer in consequence. He. first 1 commenced with pains in his; head, which gradually extended to other parts of the botiv.• " I got so _low," said Mr. Knowles, "that I was obliged to be coy cre:

• , with blankets and have a chair day. It was only then that I could feel anything like warmth. My legs got so weak that I had to have the help of a stick to get across the floor. I was terribly troubled with indiges- tion, nervous debility, and disease of the liver and kidneys, and had constant attacks of cramp in the stomach. For many weeks I suffered dreadfully, writhing in agony for hours together, and got so weak that it was painful to speak, let alone trying to move. Medicine only seemed to make me worse, and I got so that my friends gave me up

01711 NATIONAL POVERTY.

Sir,—Our legislature as it exists at present cannot and will riot amend our land laws. The great lanlowners in both houses of Parliament will not ; the Tories will not do anything to bring tie land nearer to the people ; the Vnionists dare not originate anything or sawn, anything that would not be agreeable to their masters anil leaders the Tories. Therefore, the matter must stand in abeyance until the masses, in their own inter- ests, take the matter in hand for themselves. I should strongly advise them to study this important subject, it is far more interesting anti profitable than betting on horses, dogs, or fighting men, even should they be Sullivan and Kilrain. In studying this questionthere to nothing fir the working man to dew but everything to gain. I have atriven and worked and suffered in the ranks of Radicalism and Democracy for 50 years, and at a time when to confess yourself a democrat was to be marked tins danger iris character. In that 50:yeara I have lived to see what was then considered impossible areomplislesi. We have the ballot, we have household sufferage not as perfect n• it should he. Why should we not have manhoad suffrage ? and let the man in the street vote if he is an honest man ? Lord Salisbury says "we have given the vote to the man in the know, not to site man in the etreet." Lord Salisbury never gave a vote to anyone; he reaistl to the uttermost the giving of a vote to any one. When the Borough Fran- chise Act was passed he was in the House of Commons and said that nothing of the original bill remained in theses but the word " whereas," it was so altered in committee, and if his lordship takes credit for the passing of either of those acts which gives a poor snarl the fran- chise he claims that to which he has no right or title. " We have given the vote to the man in the laturte"—na, not to the man, but to the house, to the brick and mortar, the slates and the boasts. A man may live in a house at half-a-crown a with and have a vote, but he may he burnt out, the chimney may be blown down or part of the slates be blown sit; the house becomes uninhabitable, he goes into lodgings at 3s. fld. a week but he loses his vote—the storm lias blown it away with the chimney and the elates of his roof. Is it rational. Is it equitable? No sir it is absurd. Good men in the past have suffered for endeavouring to remove these absurdities. lean well remember when many of our prisons where tenanted ba-politieiana Wheeli names are honoured now,among others Feargus O'Connor, Bronterre O'Brien, Henry Vincent, Ernest Jones, Menus Cooper, and George Lomax. Meat of those !nen did 18 months for striving for privileges we now enjoy. We must remember we have not yet arrived at the gall of justice and political perfection, no that we can take Lord Russell's advice to" rest and be thank- ful." The men whose names I hare mentioned suffered here, many others were political refugees and left the country with a price upon their heads. Frost. Williams, and Jones were sentenced at Monmontli, tube hanged, drawn, and quartered. This sentence was eommuted to transportation fir life to Van Diemens Land, since called Tasmania. I was personally acquainted with Mr. Williams' faintly he had a son stout rny age, anti I shall never forget that lad's anguish, his intense grief in parting with his father. These men laboured and suf- fered in the cause of democracy. We have entered on their Inbar% witlemt the suffering ; they have loft the world better than thev found it. It is not perfect yet— let us do our part. there are wrongs to be redressed and evils tribe eeleoVed of a formidable character. There ion Tithe Bill before Parliament not by any means in the interests of the tithepayer, but quite the reverse. If it becomes law in its present shape he is subject arid liable toarrest and imprisonment fa refusing to pay tithes; he may be proceeded against by ex.tution ! instead of distraint : he may take his pigs to market and his pigs can he impounded there and stilt' without his consent, and himself run into jail. Ile then will dis- cover that he has" brought his lava to a fine market," and all in the interests of our 11. y Mother the Church. Royal grants and royal properties want balking after. Truly aye have a glorious constitution, but we have to pay for it—perhaps a little too dear. Let us try to re- duce the cast tit just proportions. and na one will be the worse for it. It is a bad thing to have too moth money to spend—it often leads to extravagance and waste. Let an prevent it in the cause of monomy and virtue, and we shall have done am, Sir, pours res- pect fully, Sankey Bridges, 23rd Judy, 1889.

div.head: GLADSTONE.
div.p: GLADSTONE.
MR. AND MRS. GLADSTONE'S GOLDEN' WEDDING.

The golden wedding of Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone was celebrated last night, at the National Liberal Club by the presentation of a magnificent album in the name of seven thousand members of the club. The fine premises were transformed into halls of dazzling light and floral beauty, in honour of the event which has so strongly aroused the enthusiasm ot the members. The splendid river terrace, which isl6o feet long by gri feet Wide, had been roofed in with red a: I white striped canvass, the intetior being handsordy draped in blue and gold, and other Nise embellished by Hampton and Sons. Pell Mall. It was lighted temporarily by electricity, and a liberal distribution of flowers and ferns con- verted this magnificent verandah into a tropical gar- den, from which the visitors looked upon the well- kept pleaseunces of the Embankment, at present a mass of colour from geraniums, ealceolarias, and verbenas in their summer prime 'rise new London Military Band, of which Sir Arthur Sullivan is pn,- ' sident, was stationed here. Downstairs the large, smoke room, a magnificent apartment, 140 feet long hy 60 broad, and lofty in proportion, was pro- fusely decorated with dowers, and from the central settees palms rose to the ceiling, and variegated lights here, as in other parrs of the club, glowed amongst the foliage. In this room the Blue II tinge- rian Band were stationed. In the well-stoeked Gladstonian Library, which is being simiiarly deco- rated, Mr. Dan Godfrey's band performed. The din- ing, grill, large billiard, card, and committee rooms were laid out with supper-tables. An enormous quantity of cut dowers, supplied by the contrac- tor who made the Empire Theatre the wonder of a night at the Shali's recent visit, were arranged all over Ike club.

PRESENTATION TO MR. AND DRS. GLADSTONE. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone celebrate.' their "Golden Wedding" on Thursday, in quiet fashion. On returning front eight o'clock service at St. Peter's Chapel, London, in the morning, Mr. Gladstone found hanging in his morning-room a portrait of himself and his little grandson, painted by Sir J. E. Millais. Mr. Agnew, who was present, explained to the right honourable gentleman that this was a presentation to himself and Mrs. Gladstone. Though the right hon. gentleman had been sitting to Sir .f. E. Millais he had no idea for what purtose the portrait was boing painted. The likeness is I remarkably grist, and is the result of subscriptions . among persons in all classes of society, fruit the highest I to the humblest. A plate on the frame bears the follow- ing inscription A gift from English, Seottish,Welsh, and Irish women to William Ewart Gladstone and Catherine Gladstone on their golden wedding day." A vast number of congratulatory letters mid tele- gnratns besides many presents were af...n sent to Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone in recognition of their golden wedding day. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, on Thursday morning favoured Messrs. HarrauiLthewell-known photographers, with special sittings for their portraits in commemoration I of theirgolden wedding.
